title: Poster for Le Divan Japonais

image.credit: Van Gogh Museum, Netherlands; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: A colorful poster made of flat shapes of color and bold black outlines, with dark-clad figures and large hats in the foreground and a stage scene behind them. Lettering for the name of the cafe appears as part of the design.

source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, public-domain statement)

context: A lithographed poster by Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec made in 1892-1893 for a Paris cafe-concert, and now in the Van Gogh Museum in the Netherlands. The source page tags it Posters and Hats & Headwear.

descriptions.k: This is a poster for a place with music and shows. The artist used big flat shapes and dark lines. Find a big hat. Find the black shapes. What kind of show would you want to see there?
descriptions.g12: Toulouse-Lautrec made this poster in 1892 to 1893 for a cafe with music in Paris. A poster has to catch your eye from far away, so he used bold shapes, flat color and dark lines. Which shape do you notice first? What makes it stand out?
descriptions.g35: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec made this lithograph poster in 1892 to 1893 for a Paris cafe-concert, a place for songs and shows. A lithograph is printed from a design drawn on stone. Posters must be read quickly, so look at the flat colors, strong outlines and big shapes. Which choices help it grab attention from the street?
descriptions.g68: This lithograph poster by Toulouse-Lautrec (1892-1893) advertised a Paris cafe-concert. He used large flat areas of color, sharp contour and cropped figures so that the image works at a glance and from a distance. These choices were influenced by Japanese prints, as the name of the cafe suggests. How does the design make you want to look further?
descriptions.g910: Toulouse-Lautrec's lithograph poster (1892-1893) advertises a Paris cafe-concert, using flat color, sweeping outline and sharply cropped forms. The approach reflects the era's admiration for Japanese woodblock prints, hinted at by the venue's name. A poster mixes art and advertising. How does the design pursue both aims, and where might they pull against each other?
descriptions.g1112: Toulouse-Lautrec's Poster for Le Divan Japonais (1892-1893) belongs to the 1890s rise of the color lithograph as both commercial and fine art. Flat color, bold contour and cropped composition echo Japanese prints, and the form blurs lines between advertising and art. How does the poster treat the viewer as a passer-by rather than a gallery visitor, and what is gained by that?

k.daily: Look at the poster. What kind of place do you think it is for, and what would you do there?
k.emotion: How does the poster make you feel, excited, calm or something else?
k.observation: Find a big hat in the picture. What shape and color is it?
k.analysis: Which did your eyes find first, the big hat or the stage, and what pulled you there?
k.line: Trace one thick dark line with your finger. Does it curve or go straight?
k.shape: Find a big flat shape in the poster. What does it look like to you?
k.color: What colors are used in the poster? Which one stands out the most?
k.texture: A poster is printed on paper. How would the flat colors feel if you touched them?
k.space: Which people or things look close to you, and which look far away?
k.light: This poster looks like it has few shadows. How does it look different from a photograph?
k.meaning: Why do people make posters like this one for shows and places?
k.culture: Long ago, people did not have television or the internet. How might a poster tell them about a show?
k.technique: This poster is a print, not a single painting. Why might an artist make a print many times?
k.personal: If you made a poster for your favorite place, what shapes and colors would you use?
k.critical: What would you change on this poster to make it even easier to notice?

g12.daily: Why do you think the artist put the biggest shapes at the front and the stage farther back?
g12.emotion: What mood does this poster give you, lively, mysterious or something else, and which part causes it?
g12.observation: List five things you can see in the poster, from the hats to the shapes behind them.
g12.analysis: How does Toulouse-Lautrec lead your eyes from the front of the poster to the back?
g12.line: How do the bold dark outlines separate the colors, and what do they add to the poster?
g12.shape: Which shape in the poster is the biggest, and how does it help you notice the picture?
g12.color: Which colors sit next to each other in the poster, and how do they make each other look brighter?
g12.texture: The poster is made of flat color without much shading. How is that different from a painting with soft shading?
g12.space: How does the artist make a stage feel far back behind the front shapes?
g12.light: Where would you expect shadows in a real room, and how does this poster change that?
g12.meaning: What do you think the artist wanted people to feel when they walked past this poster?
g12.culture: What might a poster in 1892 tell us about how people enjoyed their evenings?
g12.technique: This poster was printed with a stone. Why is a printed picture useful for a poster?
g12.personal: What would you put in a poster for an event at your school, and how would you make it stand out?
g12.critical: What would you keep the same and what would you change if you redesigned this poster?

g35.daily: Look at the shapes and the lettering. How does the artist make the poster both a picture and an advertisement?
g35.emotion: What feelings do the dark shapes and bright colors create, and what in the poster supports your answer?
g35.observation: Study the area behind the front figures. What details can you find, and how are they simplified?
g35.analysis: How does the artist arrange the front shapes, middle and background so that your eye keeps moving?
g35.line: Where do you see thick, confident outlines, and how do they affect how the shapes look?
g35.shape: How do big, flat shapes help the poster work from far away?
g35.color: Which colors are strongest in the poster, and which do you think the artist used to balance them?
g35.texture: This lithograph has flat inks without visible brushstrokes. How does that change the surface compared with an oil painting?
g35.space: How does cropping, cutting off figures at the edge, make the space feel closer to you?
g35.light: How does the artist suggest the light of an evening show without a lot of shading?
g35.meaning: What might the large dark shapes and hats tell you about a night out in Paris around 1892?
g35.culture: The name Divan Japonais refers to Japan. How might a Paris cafe have used a Japanese theme, and what clues might you look for in the design?
g35.technique: Why do you think color lithography became popular for posters in the 1890s?
g35.personal: How would you describe this poster to a friend who had never seen it?
g35.critical: How important is a poster compared with a painting in a museum? Use details from this poster to explain your thinking.

g68.daily: Which design choices make this poster effective at a glance, and which reward a slower look?
g68.emotion: What mood do the cropped figures and dark clothing create, and how does that suit a cafe-concert?
g68.observation: Compare the level of detail in the front figures with the stage in the back. What differences do you notice?
g68.analysis: How does the placement of figures near the edge create a path toward the stage?
g68.line: How do outlines in this poster differ from the soft edges in many oil paintings of the time?
g68.shape: How do big silhouetted shapes act like a frame for the scene farther back?
g68.color: How might the limited range of flat colors help the poster read from across a street?
g68.texture: What does the printed, flat look suggest about the poster's purpose compared with a painting?
g68.space: How does the poster use overlapping and cropping to create depth without traditional perspective?
g68.light: How is evening lighting suggested here, and what might the artist have chosen to leave out?
g68.meaning: What might the choice of fashionable hats and silhouettes say about the audience the poster aimed for?
g68.culture: How might Japanese prints have influenced European artists like Toulouse-Lautrec, and what features here suggest that influence?
g68.technique: How does lithography, drawing on a stone and printing in color, make a poster like this possible?
g68.personal: What advertising techniques in this poster still appear in posters you see today?
g68.critical: When art is made to sell something, does that reduce its value as art? Use evidence from the poster in your response.

g910.daily: How does the design balance immediate impact with details that reward closer attention?
g910.emotion: How does the poster build a mood of nightlife and entertainment through shape and color rather than narrative detail?
g910.observation: Examine the way the front figures are cropped. What does the treatment suggest about the artist's compositional priorities?
g910.analysis: How does the arrangement of dark masses and bright zones create a hierarchy of attention across the sheet?
g910.line: How does the sweeping outline function as both description and graphic device?
g910.shape: How do the large, simplified silhouettes emphasize pattern and flatness over modeled volume?
g910.color: How does the restricted palette serve the practical demands of printing as well as the mood?
g910.texture: How does a lithograph's flat ink surface alter the viewer's sense of the image compared with oil painting?
g910.space: How do cropping, overlap and an elevated viewpoint replace traditional perspective in the space of the poster?
g910.light: How might the poster evoke artificial stage light and nighttime atmosphere without cast shadows?
g910.meaning: What does the poster suggest about the social world of Parisian entertainment in the early 1890s?
g910.culture: How does the Japanese reference in the venue's name connect to the wider European fascination with Japanese art, and what should we be careful about assuming?
g910.technique: How did color lithography change the possibilities for art in public spaces in this period?
g910.personal: What makes a poster memorable to you, and how well does this one meet that standard?
g910.critical: Where do you draw the line between art and advertising in this poster, and what visual evidence supports your line?

g1112.daily: How does the poster address the viewer as a passer-by, and how does its design anticipate a rapid, public mode of looking?
g1112.emotion: How far does the poster aim to convey a specific emotion rather than create an atmosphere for the venue? Weigh the visual evidence.
g1112.observation: Scan the edges where figures are cut off. What does this cropping suggest about the artist's debts to photography and Japanese prints?
g1112.analysis: How does the composition manage multiple focal points while still unifying the sheet?
g1112.line: In what ways does the outline operate as the picture's organizing principle, and what does it sacrifice?
g1112.shape: How does the reduction of figures to flat silhouettes reflect broader avant-garde interests in graphic abstraction?
g1112.color: How might the palette reflect technical constraints of color lithography as well as aesthetic aims?
g1112.texture: What is the significance of the flat printed surface for debates about whether prints and posters count as fine art?
g1112.space: How does the poster construct space through overlapping planes rather than linear perspective, and why does that matter for modernism?
g1112.light: How does the poster convey artificial light and spectacle, and what does it choose to omit?
g1112.meaning: How does the poster picture a leisure culture, and whose experience might it leave out?
g1112.culture: How should we interpret the Japanese reference in the venue's name, given the era's complicated enthusiasm for Japanese art in Europe?
g1112.technique: How did advances in color lithography in the 1890s alter the relationship between the artist, the printer and the public?
g1112.personal: How would your own encounters with advertising shape your reading of this poster as art?
g1112.critical: What would a persuasive argument look like that commercial posters like this one defined modern art more than paintings did, and how would you respond?

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Title, medium (lithography print), years (1892 to 1893), collection (Van Gogh Museum, Netherlands) and tags (Posters, Hats & Headwear) read from the arthistoryproject.com page text; no concerning terms. The source page text gives no movement; Post-Impressionism is the widely used label. The poster is for a cafe-concert, so a person should view the image to confirm the figures are suitable for K-12. Only page text was read; the image file was not visually inspected.

teacherNote.context: A color lithograph poster by Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, 1892-1893, in the Van Gogh Museum, advertising a Paris cafe-concert. The source page tags it Posters and Hats & Headwear.
directions: Have students design a poster for a school event using only flat shapes, three colors and one dark outline.
Ask students to cover part of the poster and say which shapes still carry the message.
Discuss the difference between art made to be sold and art made for a museum.
